workload.description: 600 campaign/event ingests/s fanning out to 9,600 device deliveries/s at peak

monthly_cost_per_instance.measured_context: m6i.large — AWS EC2 us-east-1 / On-Demand / Linux / shared tenancy / 730 h per month; instance-hour only (excludes EBS, data transfer); x86-64 (Intel Ice Lake). Band: zero-width: within the pinned scope the hourly list rate is a single exact published number with no variance. Month length (672-744 h), burstable credit surcharges, Savings Plans and Spot are OUT-OF-BAND modifiers, named per row, not band edges.

citations.note: $0.096/h x 730 = 7008c/month. Cross-checked to the cent against the AWS Price List Bulk API (version 20260904231117).

Band: zero-width at the Redis/Memcached standard-support rate. The Valkey engine is CHEAPER and Extended Support is DEARER; both are different products/support states, not a price range for this row, so they are named here rather than used as band edges.

db.m6i.large — AWS RDS PostgreSQL us-east-1 / On-Demand / Single-AZ (band high = Multi-AZ) / 730 h per month; INSTANCE-HOURS ONLY (excludes storage, provisioned IOPS and backup above the free allocation). Band: deployment spread: low = Single-AZ, high = Multi-AZ. Both are on-demand, standard-tier, us-east-1 PostgreSQL, so the band is fully in scope. Multi-AZ is ~2x Single-AZ.

citations.note: $0.178/h Single-AZ x 730 = 12994c/month. MySQL/MariaDB run ~3.9% cheaper than PostgreSQL for the same class. A read replica is billed as its own full instance, at the same rate as a primary.

assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 12,000 operations/s at peak. The shape that matters is the AMPLIFICATION: 600 ingested events/s become 9,600 individual device deliveries/s (~16 recipients per event). Change that ratio and the whole design resizes.

assumptions.subject: boundary
assumptions.statement: APNs, FCM, SES and Twilio are OUTSIDE this model. Keystone has no per-instance price for a third-party API, so putting one in the cost model would be an invented number. What IS modelled is the 'sender' fleet you run and pay for; the provider's own per-message fee and its rate limits are named here, not simulated. In production the provider's rate limit, not your sender fleet, is usually the real ceiling.

assumptions.subject: q
assumptions.statement: The broker is charged TWICE on the fan-out path: once to consume the campaign event and once to publish the expanded per-device messages. That is why its arrival rate exceeds the system rps.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: Delivery-log writes are BATCHED ~20:1 (visit_prob 0.05 on the deliver path). Writing one row per delivery would put ~9,600 writes/s on a single primary and saturate it — batching is the design decision that keeps this architecture standing, and it is an assumption you must actually implement.

assumptions.subject: sender
assumptions.statement: A delivery worker is sized at ~800 sends/s with a ~60 ms outbound round-trip (~48 in-flight requests per instance). It is I/O-bound waiting on the provider, not CPU-bound, so this number tracks connection concurrency more than instance size.

assumptions.subject: fanout
assumptions.statement: Fan-out workers are sized at ~400 events/s each with a ~25 ms expansion (audience query + preference filter + token lookup). A broadcast to millions of devices is a single event here and would blow through this figure — model that as a separate, much larger, workload.

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: Device tokens and the send-dedupe set live in Redis, sized for MEMORY (one entry per active device) rather than for rps — which is why its utilisation is low by design.

assumptions.subject: quiet_hours
assumptions.statement: Preference filtering, quiet hours, per-user rate caps and retry/backoff are real requirements of a notification system and are NOT modelled: the engine has no failure or scheduling model, so a retry storm after a provider outage cannot be simulated here.

_library.summary: One event fans out to thousands of device deliveries across push, SMS and email, through a durable log.
